fullText:
Summary: Aitken Spence Hotel Holdings PLC (AHUN.N0000) owns 2,676 hotel rooms, mostly in the Maldives, with resorts in Sri Lanka and hotels in Oman and India. Its profit recovered strongly to EPS of Rs 9.16 in the year to March 2026. At Rs 83.00 the share trades at 0.93x its NAV of Rs 88.89 and 11.4x trailing earnings. But its return on equity has averaged well under 10% over ten years (11.6% last year, its best), debt is about half its capital, and the April–June 2026 quarter's loss tripled as the Maldives business weakened and lease costs doubled. Weighing NAV, earnings and cash flow, the methods put fair value at about Rs 69.50, so the price is about 19% above it. I'd buy at up to about Rs 59 and treat under Rs 52 as a strong buy.

Price and key figures
Price: Rs 83.00 (CSE closing price, 2026-11-09). Please check it live. In April–June 2026 it traded between Rs 84.70 and Rs 102.75. It closed the year to March 2026 at Rs 91.60, up from Rs 80.10 a year earlier.
Three months to 30 June 2026 (group, unaudited): revenue fell 12% to Rs 9.04bn and the loss attributable to shareholders grew to Rs 972mn from Rs 351mn, a loss per share of Rs 2.89 against Rs 1.04. This is the off-season, so April–June is usually a loss, but the Maldives and Middle East businesses lost Rs 1.18bn before tax against Rs 0.21bn a year earlier.
Seasonality: most profit comes in January–March (EPS Rs 8.07 in that quarter of 2026) and October–December (Rs 3.99); April–September usually loses money.
Year to March 2026 (audited, amended annual report): revenue Rs 52.3bn (up 7%), profit before tax Rs 6.58bn (up 33%), profit attributable Rs 3.10bn, EPS Rs 9.16 (Rs 6.77), ROE 11.6%, NAV Rs 88.13, occupancy 69%, EBITDA Rs 14.8bn, interest cover 3.1x. A final dividend of Rs 0.28 a share was paid in June 2026, the first since 2019.
Debt: bank borrowings and overdrafts about Rs 34.9bn and lease liabilities Rs 23.0bn at June 2026, against Rs 12.3bn of cash and deposits. Lease liabilities more than doubled in a year (Rs 10.7bn at June 2025), so lease and interest costs are now much higher. Gearing including leases was 51% at March 2026.
Cash flow: operating cash flow was Rs 11.2bn in 2025/26 and capital spending only Rs 1.85bn, but lease payments, interest on the larger leases and catch-up spending will take a bigger share from now on.
History: EPS Rs 3.43 (2017/18), 2.37, then losses in 2019/20 (Rs -1.90) and 2020/21 (Rs -13.93, COVID), Rs 1.85, -0.94, 3.35, 6.77 and 9.16 (2025/26). ROE was 1.8% to 6% in most normal years before the last two.

Methods
NAV (Rs 88.89): 0.93x. Most of it is hotel property, much of it in US dollars in the Maldives, so a weaker rupee raises it.
Return on equity: 11.6% in 2025/26 and 10.2% in 2024/25; ten-year average well under 10%.
P/E: 11.4x trailing EPS of Rs 7.31. Year-end P/E: 10.0x (2026), 11.8x (2025).
Dividends: Rs 0.28 a year, a 0.3% yield. Not a dividend share.
NAV method (0.5x / 0.7x / 0.9x NAV): Rs 44.4 / 62.2 / 80.0, weighted Rs 60.4.
P/E method: Rs 35.0 / 67.5 / 104.5, weighted Rs 65.2.
Cash-flow DCF: Rs 43.8 / 81.0 / 145.9, weighted Rs 82.8.

Hotels' accounting profit understates their cash because depreciation is large, so a cash-flow DCF suits AHUN, but its free cash flow now has to cover much bigger lease payments. A residual-income model gives very low values (Rs 7 / 21 / 55) because ROE is below the cost of equity and almost nothing is paid out; I don't use it because it ignores the hotels' asset value. The dividend is too small for a dividend model.

Assumptions (bear / base / bull)
Cost of equity: 18% / 16.5% / 15% (a geared, seasonal business exposed to tourism shocks and currencies).
Free cash flow to shareholders this year (Rs a share): 6.0 / 8.5 / 11.0, after capital spending of about Rs 3bn and lease payments of about Rs 4bn, and after minority interests (about 31%).
Growth in the first year, fading over 10 years: 3% / 6% / 9%, to long-term 5% / 6% / 7%.
EPS for the year to March 2027 × P/E: 5.0 × 7 / 7.5 × 9 / 9.5 × 11.
NAV multiple: 0.5x / 0.7x / 0.9x.
Average of the three methods: Rs 41.1 / Rs 70.2 / Rs 110.1.
Common: Sri Lankan government bonds yield about 11–12%. The base case assumes this year's EPS falls to about Rs 7.50 because of the weaker first quarter and higher lease costs.

Fair value and buy price
Fair value: weighting 30/50/20 gives about Rs 69.50 (0.8x NAV), so Rs 83.00 is about 19% above it.
Buy price: a 15% margin of safety gives Rs 59.00, and 25% gives Rs 52.10.
Plan for 500 shares: 200 at up to Rs 69.50, 150 at up to Rs 59.00 and 150 at up to Rs 52.10. That averages about Rs 61.13, about Rs 30,565, against Rs 41,500 at Rs 83.00.
Realism: Rs 69.50 needs about a 16% fall. The share was Rs 66.20 in March 2024 and Rs 75 within the last year (broker's 52-week low), so the first tier is possible in a weak market; Rs 59 and below would need a tourism setback.

Sensitivity (DCF base case, Rs per share)
Cost of equity 15%: 66.7 / 94.4 / 122.2 for free cash flow of Rs 6.0 / 8.5 / 11.0 a share.
Cost of equity 16.5%: 57.1 / 81.0 / 104.8.
Cost of equity 18%: 50.0 / 70.8 / 91.7.

What would change my view
Supports a higher value: Maldives occupancy and room rates recovering; tourist arrivals to Sri Lanka growing strongly; ROE staying above 11%; debt falling; a weaker rupee lifting dollar earnings; a higher dividend.
Supports a lower value: more losses in the Maldives; higher lease and interest costs eating the cash flow; a travel shock (conflict, health scare, fuel prices); a stronger rupee; heavy spending to refurbish older resorts.

These are my estimates from the annual reports for the years to March 2025 and March 2026 (amended version) and the interim reports to June 2026. The interim figures are unaudited, so check the price before ordering. This is analysis, not personal financial advice.
